title: Drop the k-th From the End
statement:
You get the head of a singly linked list and a number k. Remove the k-th node counting from the end, where k = 1 is the last node, and return the head of the resulting list.

k is always between 1 and the length of the list. The node you remove may be the head itself.

Lists are written as arrays: [3, 8] is 3 → 8. An empty result is null (shown as []).

examples.why: Counting from the end: 2 is first, 6 is second. To remove 6, node 1 must point at 2.
The 5th from the end of a 5-node list is the head. There is no node before it to relink, so the head itself changes.
Removing the only node leaves an empty list.

hints: If you knew the length L, which node from the front would you remove? Which node do you actually need to stand on to remove it?
To do it in one pass, keep two pointers with a fixed gap between them. When the front one reaches the end, where is the back one?
Start both pointers at a dummy node placed before the head. Move the front one k steps, then move both until the front one is on the last node. The back one is now just before the node to remove.

explain.intuition:
To unlink a node in a singly linked list you have to stand on the node before it. The k-th from the end is the (L − k + 1)-th from the front, so you could count the length first and walk again. That is two passes and perfectly fine.

The one-pass version uses a ruler of fixed length. Put two pointers k nodes apart and slide them together. When the leading pointer stands on the last node, the trailing pointer is k nodes behind it, which is exactly the node before the one to remove. A dummy node before the head gives the trailing pointer somewhere to stand when the head itself has to go, so that case needs no special code.
steps: Create dummy with dummy.next = head. Set lead = trail = dummy.
While lead.next is not null, move both lead and trail one step.
Now trail.next is the node to remove: set trail.next = trail.next.next.
Return dummy.next, not head: the head may have been removed.
pitfalls: Off by one on the gap: moving lead k + 1 times, or stopping when lead is null instead of on the last node, removes the neighbour of the right node.
Returning head. When k equals the length, the head is the node removed, and the answer starts at the second node.
Not handling a one-node list: without a dummy, there is no previous node to relink.

solutions.title: Count, then walk
solutions.idea: First pass counts the length L. Second pass stops on node L − k (counting the dummy as 0) and skips the node after it.

solutions.title: Two pointers k apart
solutions.idea: Move a lead pointer k steps ahead of a trailing one, then move both until lead is on the last node. Trail is then right before the node to remove.

followups: k may now be larger than the length, in which case nothing is removed. How do you detect that in the one-pass version?
Return the middle node in one pass with the same two-pointer idea. What is the gap now?
